section.title: Love One Another
section.sectionRationale: John presses the message heard from the beginning: love one another. He sets Cain, who hated and murdered, against Jesus, who laid down His life, and shows that real love acts sacrificially. Such love assures our hearts before God, and John ties it to the twofold command to believe in the Son and love one another, sealed by the Spirit.
section.thesis: Love one another is the message from the beginning, and it is defined not by Cain's murderous hatred but by Jesus laying down His life, so that love shown in costly action assures our hearts before God, who commands us to believe in His Son and love one another, and who abides in us by His Spirit.
section.frameNote: Four beats: the message to love, with Cain as the anti-pattern; love defined by the cross and shown in action; hearts assured before God; and the command to believe and love, sealed by the Spirit.

verses.text: This is the message you have heard from the beginning: We should {{agapao|love}} one another.
Do not be like Cain, who belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did Cain slay him? Because his own deeds were evil, while those of his brother were righteous.
So do not be surprised, brothers, if the world hates you.
We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love our brothers. The one who does not love remains in death.
Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that eternal life does not reside in a murderer.
By this we know what love is: Jesus {{tithemi|laid down}} His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.
If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the {{agape|love}} of God abide in him?
Little children, let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth.

units.label: Hearts assured before God
units.note: God is greater than our hearts

verses.text: And by this we will know that we belong to the truth, and will assure our hearts in His presence:
Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things.
Beloved, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have {{parrhesia|confidence}} before God,
and we will receive from Him whatever we ask, because we keep His commandments and do what is pleasing in His sight.
And this is His {{entole|commandment}}: that we should believe in the name of His Son, Jesus Christ, and we should love one another just as He commanded us.
Whoever keeps His commandments remains in God, and God in him. And by this we know that He remains in us: by the {{pneuma|Spirit}} He has given us.

agapao.gloss: To love, to seek another's good with self-giving devotion. The command to love one another is the message heard from the beginning. It is not mere sentiment but active goodwill that shows itself in deeds, the very opposite of Cain's hatred.

tithemi.gloss: To lay down, place, set. Jesus laid down His life for us, freely giving Himself to death. The same verb appears in John's Gospel where Jesus lays down His life for the sheep. It defines love at its deepest and sets the pattern His people follow toward one another.

agape.gloss: Love, self-giving love that seeks the good of another. The love of God, whether His love in us or love that comes from Him, cannot truly abide in someone who closes his heart to a brother in need. Real agape opens the hand as well as the mouth.

parrhesia.gloss: Confidence, boldness, freedom of speech. When our hearts do not condemn us, we have boldness before God, especially in prayer. It is the freedom of a child before a loving Father, not the arrogance of the self-assured, and it flows from belonging to the truth.

entole.gloss: Commandment, charge, instruction. John sums up God's commandment as two joined things: believe in the name of His Son and love one another. Faith in Christ and love for others are not rivals but a single command, the shape of the life that abides in God.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, breath, wind. The Holy Spirit whom God has given is the inner witness that God abides in us. The Spirit both assures believers of their union with God and empowers the obedient, loving life that gives outward evidence of it.

basic.context: The message from the very beginning is simple and hard: love one another. John holds up two opposite examples. Cain hated his righteous brother and murdered him; Jesus loved us and laid down His life. Real love is not just words but action, like sharing with a brother in need. This kind of love assures our hearts that we belong to God, and even when our conscience accuses us, God is greater than our hearts. He commands us to believe in Jesus and love each other, and He gives His Spirit as the seal that He lives in us.
basic.hermeneutics: John continues the test of true faith, now focused on love shown in deeds. He is not making love the payment for salvation but the evidence of it: we know we have passed from death to life because we love. The famous words of verses 19 and 20 comfort troubled believers, God is greater than our accusing hearts, while the whole passage still warns that a loveless life is a sign of death, not life.
basic.originalLanguages: The message is to love, agapao, one another. Love is defined by the cross: Jesus laid down, tithemi, His life for us. The love, agape, of God cannot abide in one who shuts his heart to a brother in need. When our hearts do not condemn us we have confidence, parrhesia, before God. His commandment, entole, is to believe and love, and He abides in us by the Spirit, pneuma, He has given.
basic.typology: Cain and Abel, the first brothers, become the pattern of the world's hatred for the righteous, fulfilled supremely when the world hated and killed Jesus, the truly righteous One. Jesus laying down His life fulfils the sacrificial love foreshadowed in the offerings and defines love for all who follow Him.
basic.christ: Jesus is the definition of love: He laid down His life for us, and His self-giving is both the ground of our new life and the pattern for ours. He is the Son in whose name we are commanded to believe, and He commands us to love one another as He has loved us.
basic.god: God is the one who commands love and defines it by His Son's sacrifice. He is greater than our accusing hearts, knowing all things, and He gives His Spirit as the inner assurance that He abides in us. He is both the judge before whom we stand and the Father who gives us confidence.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 4 records Cain and Abel. John 15:13 says greater love has no one than to lay down his life. John 13:34 gives the command to love as Jesus loved, and Romans 8 speaks of the Spirit witnessing that we are God's children.
basic.oneStory: From the first brothers the world has been divided between hatred and love, Cain and Abel. The whole story turns on the righteous One, Jesus, who was hated and yet laid down His life in love. Now His people, born of God and sealed by the Spirit, are called to that same self-giving love, the mark of those who have passed from death to life.

context.literary:
The second half of chapter 3 is built on a series of contrasts that John sets one against another. The opening verse of the section restates the 'message' of the letter, which he has used for the first time in 1:5 for the message that God is light. Here the message is that we should love one another, and the whole passage unpacks that message in four moves. Verses 11 to 15 give the negative pattern in Cain and the world's hatred. Verses 16 to 18 give the positive pattern in Christ and the shape of love in action. Verses 19 to 22 turn to the believer's conscience and prayer. Verses 23 and 24 close with the one commandment and the sign of the Spirit.

The section moves between three kinds of knowing. Verse 14 says 'we know that we have passed from death to life,' verse 16 says 'by this we know what love is,' and verse 19 says 'by this we will know that we belong to the truth.' Each of these 'we know' sentences gives a ground and a result, and together they carry the letter's central purpose of giving assurance, 5:13. Alongside them runs the vocabulary of the heart. Verse 17 speaks of shutting up one's compassion, verses 19 to 21 of our hearts condemning or not condemning, and the whole is a study of what happens inside a person who loves or fails to.

The language is bound together by a pair of terms that work as a hinge in the middle. In verse 16 Jesus laid down His 'life,' a word for the whole person, and in verse 17 the question concerns 'earthly possessions,' a word for material livelihood. The step from one to the other is deliberate: if love is meant to give a life, how can it refuse a loaf? Verse 18 draws the lesson, with a contrast between 'word and speech' and 'action and truth,' and the passage proceeds from there to the settling of the conscience and the answering of prayer.
context.historical:
The story of Cain and Abel in Genesis 4 was familiar to every Jewish reader and to Gentile converts who had learned the Scriptures, and it had already acquired a standing as the pattern of the violent man who hates the righteous. Jesus had spoken of the 'blood of righteous Abel,' Matthew 23:35, and the letter to the Hebrews says that Abel by faith still speaks, Hebrews 11:4. John uses the story to say what the world's hatred is rooted in. Cain did not kill because of a quarrel over property. He killed because his brother's deeds exposed his own, and John says that this is what lies beneath the world's hostility to believers.

The setting for the call to share possessions was a society with no public safety net. A brother or sister who lost work, or whose breadwinner died, could be left with nothing. The early church had met this need by sharing, Acts 4:32 to 35, and by gifts between congregations, 2 Corinthians 8 and 9. James had written that a word of blessing without provision of food and clothing is worth nothing, James 2:15 and 16. John's readers would have recognised the situation in verse 17, and they would have felt its force, since many of them were themselves poor or under pressure from the surrounding city.

There was also the pressure of the divided community. People who had left had been among the fellowship, and hatred, suspicion and recrimination can follow such a division. John's remarks about hate and murder have this in view. He does not accuse them of killing, but of the root that Jesus taught in the Sermon on the Mount, that anger and contempt are of the same family as murder, Matthew 5:21 and 22. The 'brother' whom he has in mind is, in the first place, a fellow believer, the person next to you in the meeting.
context.canonical:
The passage knits together three of the largest themes in Scripture. The first is the command to love, which in the Old Testament is a command to love one's neighbour, Leviticus 19:18, and which Jesus made the sign of discipleship: 'a new commandment I give you: Love one another. As I have loved you, so you also must love one another,' John 13:34 and 35. John calls this 'the message you have heard from the beginning,' and in 2:7 and 8 he says it is both old and new. The greatest example is stated in John 15:13, 'Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends,' and in John 10:11 and 17 and 18, where Jesus says the good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep. John's verb in 3:16 is the same one the Gospel uses in those verses.

The second theme is the contrast of the two brothers. After Genesis 4, Abel's blood cries out from the ground, Genesis 4:10, and Hebrews sets it against the blood of Jesus, which speaks a better word, Hebrews 12:24. John 8:44 says the devil was a murderer from the beginning, and 1 John 3:15 uses the same word for the one who hates his brother. The third theme is the way of assurance. Hebrews 10:22 invites believers to draw near with full assurance, hearts sprinkled to cleanse a guilty conscience, and 1 John 5:14 and 15 returns to the confidence of asking according to His will. Romans 8:16 says that the Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's children, which is close to 3:24.

The passage is further connected to the second half of the letter by 4:7 to 21, which takes up verses 16 and 17 and shows that love has its source in God's own love, so that to love the brother is to share in that.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John wanted his readers to be able to tell the difference between a love that is real and one that is only claimed, and he gives them a test that cannot be faked for long: what do you do when a brother or sister is in need? He is blunt that speech alone does not count, but he is not trying to make them anxious. The passage that follows is designed to calm the conscience of the person who has a genuine but imperfect love. Hearts that accuse us are not the last word, because God is greater than our hearts.

He also wanted them to see that love has a definition and a standard, and that the standard is Christ's death. Much of what passed as love in the surrounding world was a matter of affection among friends or a calculated exchange of favours. John tells them that it is a laying down of life, which makes it costly and public. In the same breath he gives them an explanation for the hatred they are meeting. The world hated Abel and killed him, and the world will treat the church in a similar way. They should not be surprised, and they should not repay it in kind.

Finally, John wanted to restate the single commandment that holds the whole life of faith together, to believe in the name of the Son and to love one another. The two cannot be separated, and a community that holds only one of them has lost both.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Most of this passage is prescriptive, but the key terms have to be handled with care. The call to lay down our lives for the brothers, verse 16, is a statement of what love ought to look like and not a requirement that every believer seek martyrdom. John gives the practical form in the very next verse, the sharing of possessions with someone in need. Taken together, the two verses show that sacrifice includes both the extreme case and the ordinary one, and that the ordinary one is where most of us will be tested.

The description of Cain is a record of what happened and a warning that the same root is available to every heart. It is not a statement that anyone who feels anger toward a fellow believer is already a murderer, but a claim about the direction of hatred. Verses 19 to 22 also need care: they describe the confidence of someone whose heart does not condemn, and the promise that prayer is answered, 'because we keep His commandments,' is a description of the life of a person in fellowship with God and not a formula that guarantees any particular request. It should be read with 5:14, where asking is 'according to His will.'

debates.question: What does 'God is greater than our hearts' mean in verse 20?

views.label: A word of comfort
views.case: Most readers take the verse as assurance. When conscience accuses a genuine believer of falling short, God, who knows all things including the sincerity of our love, is greater than that accusation and is more merciful than our self-reproach. On this view 'because' in verses 19 and 20 gives the reason we can be assured: God's knowledge includes what our conscience cannot see. This fits the pastoral purpose of the letter, 5:13.

views.label: A word of warning
views.case: Others take the verse as a sterner statement: if our hearts condemn us, we should take it seriously, because God, who knows all things, will judge more severely than we do. On this reading the verse supports John's argument that love must be visible in action and cannot rest on feeling. The difficulty is that verse 21 speaks of confidence when the heart does not condemn, and that tone seems to set a contrast with verse 20 as relief.

views.label: Condemnation corrected by greater knowledge
views.case: A third view holds that the heart may condemn wrongly, as it can, and God's greater knowledge corrects it. Our hearts do not always judge accurately, and God sees both the failures and the real faith, and He alone knows the whole truth about us.

debates.bearing: The comfort reading fits the context best, because verse 19 says the purpose is to 'assure our hearts.' Even so, the warning is not lost, since the passage requires that a person's love be real in deed, and the one who has no such love has nothing to be assured about.

debates.question: Who are 'the brothers' that we are to love?

views.label: Fellow believers
views.case: John's word 'brother' throughout the letter is used for a fellow member of the family of God, as in 2:9 to 11 and 4:20 and 21, where loving God and loving the brother are joined. The first object of the command is the church, which is the community under pressure and the one that Jesus said would be known by its love, John 13:35.

views.label: Everyone in need
views.case: Others argue that the example of Cain's brother and Jesus' death for the world, 2:2, point to a wider love, and that the Bible elsewhere requires love of neighbour and even of enemies, Matthew 5:44. They say it is unlikely that John would exclude those outside the church from compassion.

debates.bearing: The two views need not collide. John's focus is on the believing community, where love is first learned and tested, but nothing in the passage forbids the same love from reaching beyond it. The Lord who laid down His life did so for the whole world, and those who follow Him will not draw the line narrower than He did.

study.originalLanguages:
The word John uses in verse 11 for 'message,' angelia, links back to 1:5, 'This is the message we have heard from Him and declare to you: God is light.' In both places it introduces a summary of the gospel's demand, first about the character of God and now about the conduct of His people. In verse 12 John says Cain 'slew' his brother, using a verb, sphazo, that means to slaughter, and not the ordinary word for kill. The same verb is used of the Lamb in Revelation 5:6, 'a Lamb who appeared to have been slain.' The effect is a stark contrast: the first brother was butchered by hatred, while the Lamb was slain by love.

In verse 14 'we have passed' translates a perfect verb, metabebekamen, with the sense 'we have crossed over and stand on the other side.' Jesus uses the same verb in John 5:24, 'he has crossed over from death to life.' The perfect tense marks a completed move with a lasting result. In verse 15 the word for 'murderer,' anthropoktonos, is the term Jesus uses for the devil in John 8:44, so that to hate a brother is to share a family trait with the one who was a murderer from the beginning.

The verb tithemi in verse 16, 'laid down,' is the verb Jesus uses of the good shepherd who 'lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11, and of Himself in John 10:17 and 18, where it is a deliberate act of authority. John adds that the object is psyche, the person's life as a living being. That makes a contrast with the word in verse 17 for 'earthly possessions,' bios, which means a person's material means. In verse 17 the compassion is literally the splanchna, the inward parts, the seat of feeling in Greek speech, and the verb for 'withholds' is literally 'shuts,' as if one locked the gate of one's own heart.

Verse 18 sets 'word and speech' against 'action and truth.' The Greek reads literally 'in word or tongue,' and the contrast is between talk and what is done, with 'truth' showing that real love is a genuine thing and not a pretence. In verses 19 to 21 the word 'heart,' kardia, is the whole inner life of a person, including conscience, and the confidence of verse 21, parrhesia, is freedom to speak openly before God. John uses it again for the day of judgment in 4:17 and for prayer in 5:14.

The 'commandment' of verse 23 is singular, entole, and it contains two parts in one sentence: that we should believe in the name of His Son and love one another. The believing is put in a form that sees it as a single act of trust, and the loving in a form that continues, which suits a decision that begins a life of love. The 'name' means the person with all that He is. Finally, 'remains,' meno, in verse 24, is again the letter's word for abiding, and the Spirit is the sign of it, as in 4:13.

typology.type: Cain and Abel, the two brothers and the two ways
typology.fulfillment: Genesis 4 sets a righteous brother against one who hated him, and Abel's blood cries out from the ground, Genesis 4:10. John makes Cain the pattern of the world, and Abel the pattern of the righteous who are hated. The pattern is fulfilled in Jesus, the truly righteous One, whom the world hated and killed, John 15:18 and 19. The escalation is that Abel's blood cried out for justice, while the blood of Jesus 'speaks a better word,' Hebrews 12:24, one of mercy and forgiveness. The type falls short because Abel was a righteous man and not a sinless one, and his death did not save anyone.

typology.type: The good shepherd who lays down His life
typology.fulfillment: The Old Testament calls God and His chosen rulers shepherds of the flock, and condemns the shepherds who feed themselves, as in Ezekiel 34. Jesus says, 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11, and John's verb in 3:16 is the same. The correspondence is that a shepherd's care includes risking his life, and in Christ that risk becomes a real death freely accepted, John 10:18. The escalation is from a human shepherd who might die defending the flock to the Shepherd who dies in the place of the flock. The type falls short in that earthly shepherds do not rise again by their own authority, but He took up His life again.

The offerings of the Law showed that life is given in the place of life, and the blood of the sacrifice cleansed and covered, Leviticus 17:11. John does not use sacrificial vocabulary in 3:16, but he says Jesus laid down His life for us, and elsewhere in the letter He is called the atoning sacrifice for our sins, 2:2 and 4:10. The cross is the fulfilment of the pattern: a life given, willingly and once for all, Hebrews 10:10. The pattern also passes to believers, who are to 'walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering,' Ephesians 5:2. The type falls short in that the believer's self-giving is an imitation and not an atonement.

study.christ:
The passage places Christ at the centre of the definition of love, and John gives no other. 'By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us.' Before the cross, love in the ancient world could be described but not defined by any single act. After it, John says, we have an event to point to, and the word is filled with its meaning. That is also why 4:10 says that love consists not in our love for God but in His sending of the Son as the atoning sacrifice. Christ's death is both the proof of the Father's love and the example for ours.

John's use of the verb tithemi carries the voice of Jesus Himself. He said, 'I lay down My life in order to take it up again. No one takes it from Me, but I lay it down of My own accord,' John 10:17 and 18. John's readers would have heard in verse 16 an echo of these words, and with them the claim that the death was a deliberate act of the Son and not a defeat. The same love was the one the Father showed in sending Him, 4:9 and 10, so that the whole movement from the Father through the Son to the believers' love for each other is one continuous love.

The passage also shows Christ as the righteous One whose life was hated. Cain killed his brother because his brother's deeds were righteous. In the Gospels, Jesus says that the world hated Him first, John 15:18, and Hebrews sets His blood against the blood of Abel, Hebrews 12:24. The pattern is carried further in Matthew 23:35, where the blood of righteous Abel is the first in a long line of the righteous slain. Jesus belongs to that line, and in Him the line culminates, since His death is the one that achieves what none of the others could.

Christ is also the giver of the commandment. The 'commandment' of verse 23 is the one that He gave, and John 13:34 describes it as new because the standard is now 'as I have loved you.' To believe in the name of Jesus and to love as He loved are two aspects of one allegiance. Finally, the Spirit by whom we know that He abides in us is the Spirit that Jesus promised, John 14:16 and 17.

The caution is that John does not say believers atone for each other's sins by laying down their lives. The comparison in verse 16 is of attitude and direction, 'we ought to,' and not of equal power. Only His death takes away sin, and our love follows it.
study.god:
The God of this passage is the one who is greater than our hearts. That short sentence says something about both His knowledge and His mercy. 'He knows all things' means that He sees what we cannot: the sincerity beneath the failures, the real faith under the accusing conscience. A God who knew less than we do about ourselves would be no comfort, since we could never be sure that we had been fairly judged. A God who knows everything can be trusted to judge justly, and the same knowledge is a ground of peace for the believer.

The passage also shows God as the one who defines love and gives it. John does not say that love is a human achievement that God admires, but that God has shown what it is, by giving His Son. The love that believers are to show is derived from the love of God, which is why 4:7 says that love comes from God and that everyone who loves has been born of God. The God of Scripture is a God of self-giving love who does not stand aloof from His creatures. The Father gave the Son, and the Son gave Himself.

The passage shows God as a hearer of prayer. Verse 22 says we receive from Him whatever we ask, because we keep His commandments and do what pleases Him. That does not make God a machine that dispenses requests. It rests on the covenant relationship in which a child who loves the Father asks for what the Father wants, and 5:14 states the limit in the phrase 'according to His will.' The God who hears is a Father and not a servant.

God is also the one who gives the Spirit as a sign and seal of His dwelling in us. Verse 24 says we know that He remains in us by the Spirit He has given. That is the doctrine of God's indwelling presence, and it is the New Testament counterpart of the promise that God would put His Spirit within His people, Ezekiel 36:27. The Spirit is not an impersonal force but the way the Father and the Son are present in the believer.

For worship, the passage gives a way to hold together honesty and confidence. We may bring our accusing hearts to God because He is greater, and we may bring our requests because He is a Father. And we show that we have met Him by giving to those in need what He has first given to us.

crossReferences.note: The story John has in mind: Cain's offering is not accepted, he grows angry, and God warns that sin is crouching at the door. It shows that hatred begins in the heart and not at the moment of the blow, which is why John can say that hating a brother is already murder.

Jesus teaches that anger and contempt toward a brother are of the same family as murder and bring judgment. It gives the teaching behind John's claim in verse 15 and shows that he is drawing on the Lord's own words.

The new commandment to love as Jesus loved, which makes love the mark of discipleship before the world. John's 'message from the beginning' is this commandment, and the standard in both is the love of Christ.

In the upper room Jesus names giving up one's life for friends as the highest love. It is the saying John applies in verse 16, and it shows that the call to lay down our lives comes from Jesus' own definition of love.
Jesus is the good shepherd who lays down His life and takes it up again of His own accord. It explains the verb of verse 16 and shows that the cross was a free act of love and not a defeat.

James says that a kind word to a brother without clothes or food, with no help given, is of no use. It is the clearest New Testament parallel to verses 17 and 18 and shows that the early church understood love as practical provision.

The love of God was revealed in sending His Son, and if God so loved us, we ought to love one another. It gives the foundation for verse 16: our love is a response to His, and the example of Christ rests on the Father's gift.
Confidence in prayer rests on asking according to His will. It qualifies the promise of verse 22 and shows that the answered prayer of a loving believer is prayer that shares the Father's purposes.
The blood of Jesus speaks a better word than the blood of Abel. It sets the two righteous deaths side by side and shows that the second answers the cry of the first with mercy.
The Spirit Himself testifies with our spirit that we are God's children. It parallels verse 24, where the Spirit is the sign of God's indwelling, and shows the Spirit's role in giving assurance.

study.oneStory:
The first murder in the Bible is the murder of a brother, and the story shows that the break with God in Genesis 3 quickly became a break between people. Cain's hatred of Abel is the first fruit of the fall, and 1 John 3 treats it as the pattern for the world's treatment of those who belong to God. From Abel to the prophets and on to Jesus, righteous blood is shed, as Jesus Himself says in Matthew 23:35. The long conflict between the line of the serpent and the line of the woman, Genesis 3:15, is a conflict over love and hatred.

God's answer is to create a family of those who love. Israel is told to love the neighbour as itself, Leviticus 19:18, and the prophets denounce the failure of that love in the neglect of the poor. In Jesus the love of God is shown in its completeness: He lays down His life, and rises, and gives the Spirit. The church that results is meant to be a community in which the world can see what the love of God looks like, John 13:35. John's readers, under pressure and divided, are being called to be that community.

The passage holds together the 'already' and the 'not yet' of the story. We have already passed from death to life, and the proof is love. Yet we still live in a world where hatred wins battles and hearts accuse us. The confidence of verse 21 is a foretaste of the confidence we will have on the last day, 4:17, and the Spirit who now assures us is the guarantee of what is coming.

The end of the story answers the story of Cain. In the new creation, there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4, and the family of God will live in the presence of the Father without fear. The murder that opened the story of human history will have no successor, and love that began as a commandment will be the air that the redeemed breathe. Between now and then, each act of costly love is a sign that the new age has begun, and each refusal of love is a reminder of how much of the old one remains.

sermon.title: Loving One Another
sermon.why: Begg preaches this passage, 1 John 3:11-18, on the message to love, Cain versus the love of Christ, and love shown in action and truth. A clear, orthodox handling of love as the mark of those who have passed from death to life.

quiz.q: Why does John hold up Cain as a warning in verse 12?

options.text: Because Cain hated and murdered his righteous brother, the opposite of the love we are called to.
options.note: Cain is the anti-pattern: hatred of a righteous brother, springing from evil deeds.

options.text: Because Cain was punished more harshly than he deserved.
options.note: John's point is Cain's hatred, not the justice of his punishment.

options.text: Because Cain simply made a careless mistake.
options.note: It was deliberate hatred and murder, not a mere mistake.

options.text: Because Cain worked hard but was overlooked.
options.note: The issue is that his deeds were evil and he hated his righteous brother, not that he was overlooked.

quiz.q: How does John define what love is in verse 16?

options.text: Jesus laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.
options.note: Love is defined by Christ's self-sacrifice and patterned for His people.

options.text: Love is mainly a warm feeling toward others.
options.note: John defines love by sacrificial action, not feeling alone.

options.text: Love is saying kind words when convenient.
options.note: John insists on love in action and truth, not word and speech only.

options.text: Love is admiring good people from a distance.
options.note: Real love gives itself for others, as Jesus did, not merely admires them.

quiz.q: What does verse 17 say about love and a brother in need?

options.text: Shutting your heart to a brother in need shows the love of God does not abide in you.
options.note: Real love opens the hand; withholding compassion contradicts the love of God.

options.text: Helping the needy is optional for spiritual people.
options.note: John makes practical compassion a test of genuine love, not an option.

options.text: Only feelings of pity matter, not action.
options.note: John calls for action and truth, not feelings that never move to help.

options.text: Generosity earns your salvation.
options.note: Generosity is evidence of God's love abiding, not the purchase of salvation.

quiz.q: What does John mean that 'God is greater than our hearts' when our hearts condemn us?

options.text: For those who love in deed and truth, God's gracious verdict outweighs an accusing conscience.
options.note: In context it comforts believers whose genuine love may not still every fear.

options.text: God overlooks sin so we need never examine ourselves.
options.note: John still calls for real love; it is not license to ignore sin.

options.text: Our feelings are the final measure of our standing with God.
options.note: The point is the opposite; God, not our fluctuating hearts, is the measure.

options.text: God's greater knowledge only ever condemns us further.
options.note: That is one sobering edge, but the primary aim here is assurance for those who love genuinely.

quiz.q: What is God's commandment, according to verse 23?

options.text: To believe in the name of His Son, Jesus Christ, and to love one another.
options.note: John joins faith in the Son and love for one another into a single command.

options.text: To believe correct doctrine without loving anyone.
options.note: Faith and love are bound together; belief without love is incomplete.

options.text: To love others while it does not matter what you believe.
options.note: Love matters, but so does believing in the name of the Son; both are commanded.

options.text: To keep a long list of rituals to earn favour.
options.note: The command is faith in Christ and love, not ritual to earn favour.

questions: The message from the beginning is to love one another. Who is the brother or sister God is calling you to love in action, not just in words, this week?
Love is defined by Jesus laying down His life. What would laying down your life, your time, comfort, or resources, look like for someone in your church or family?
John ties love to sharing with a brother in material need. Is there a need you have seen but passed by, and how might you respond with real compassion?
When your heart condemns you, God is greater than your heart. How does it help to know that God's gracious knowledge of you outweighs your accusing conscience?
God's command joins believing in Jesus and loving one another. Do you tend to emphasise one of these over the other, and how can you hold them together?

translationNotes.note: 'Laid down His life' uses the verb tithemi, the same expression John's Gospel uses for the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, John 10:11.
The Greek is compressed and can be read in more than one way; the sense is that genuine love assures the heart, and that God, who knows all, is greater than a self-condemning conscience.
'His commandment' is singular yet contains two parts, believing in the Son and loving one another, showing that John treats faith and love as one inseparable charge.
